result.summary: Zeus, grown up, uses Metis's drug to make Cronus disgorge his swallowed children, then wins the war against the Titans with the freed Cyclopes and Hundred-handers. The gods draw lots for rule, and the passage then lists the offspring of the Titans, Sea and Earth, and Nereus.

scenes.title: Zeus overthrows the Titans
scenes.summary: Metis drugs Cronus so he vomits up the children. Zeus frees those in Tartarus, gains thunderbolt, helmet and trident, defeats the Titans and the brothers draw lots for rule.
scenes.stakes: Zeus and his siblings risk defeat by Cronus and the Titans and the loss of any share in power.

scenes.title: Genealogies of the Titans and sea
scenes.summary: A catalogue of the children of the Titans, of Sea and Earth, and of Nereus, including Atlas, Prometheus, Chiron, Hecate, Iris and the Nereids. Zeus honors Styx with the oath.

alias_notes.explanation: Pontus is the Greek name for Sea.

notable_quotes.reason: Explains why the gods swear oaths by the water of Styx.

analysis.text: Zeus's rise follows succession myth: power passes by violence and alliance, with the freed prisoners securing victory.
The genealogies organize Greek divine figures and natural forces into a single family tree, as in Hesiod's Theogony.

legacy.text: The Titanomachy shaped later Greek and Roman art and literature, and the name Titan became a word for the colossal.

fun_facts.text: The Library, attributed to Apollodorus, is a prose handbook of Greek myth, and this passage closely follows Hesiod's Theogony.

language_notes.text: "Disgorge" means to vomit up or expel what has been swallowed.
"Jailoress" is a female jailer; Campe guarded the Cyclopes and Hundred-handers in Tartarus.
"Sovereignty" and "dominion" mean rule; "cast lots" means drew lots to decide by chance.
"Oaths to be sworn by the water of Styx" refers to the gods' most binding oath, taken on this river.
The author promises to return to the Gorgons in the story of Perseus, a later section of this work.

context_notes.text: Cronus swallowed his children at birth, fearing a prophecy that one would overthrow him. The stone was given him in place of Zeus.
Pluto is the god of the underworld, here ruling Hades. The Cyclopes were one-eyed smith-giants, and their gifts became the brothers' emblems.
Atlas was condemned to hold up the sky. Prometheus is famed for stealing fire for humankind.
Chiron was the wise centaur who tutored heroes. Hecate is a goddess linked with magic and night.

literary_notes.text: The division of the universe sets up the structure of the Olympian order that later myths assume.
Victory, Dominion, Emulation and Violence are abstract forces presented as children of Pallas and Styx.
The long list of Nereid names gives the passage an epic, genealogical sweep, as in Homer and Hesiod.
